Maladaptive Strategies.value: I dwell on what I have done wrong
never allow myself to feel or express anger
I avoid eating or restrict food as a way of coping

Threat.value: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening
I wake during the night to check whether I am safe
Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it

Memory.value: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over
When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop
When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event

Negative Appraisals.value: You can never know who will harm you

vignette: The violence peaked on a damp October night when Dinh Tran’s former partner, a man whose quiet demeanor had slowly curdled into control, dragged him into the rear seat of a taxi. Mark pinned him against the cracked vinyl, striking his ribs and jaw until Dinh gasped and accepted the demand for silence, the confined space and the rhythm of the tires fusing into a single, inescapable moment. Years later, as a municipal journalist chasing city hall deadlines, a packed bus or a stranger’s proximity in a newsroom elevator would instantly hijack his nervous system. When these trauma-related events occurred, the memory of the taxi did not recede into the past but surged forward with violent immediacy, accompanied by a sharp, familiar ache in his ribs and jaw that forced him to step off the bus mid-route or flee the elevator. This vivid return of the assault made the present feel perpetually dangerous, cementing his conviction that he was inadequate and that people could not be trusted. His belief that harm could strike without warning then shaped his avoidance, steering him away from solo interviews and causing him to leave newsroom briefings whenever another man entered the room alone. As the weeks bled into months, these encounters quickly birthed new coping habits that felt necessary for survival. When the bus doors closed or a male colleague approached his desk, Dinh suppressed any spark of rage and forced himself to ruminate on his own perceived failures, convincing himself that staying quiet and unobtrusive was the only way to prevent another assault. To steady his hands during these encounters, he began restricting his food intake, telling himself that hunger would keep him sharp and invisible. Yet the very strategies he adopted to navigate the day quietly hardened his worldview. By constantly blaming himself and stifling his anger, Dinh’s confidence eroded further, cementing his conviction that he was fundamentally inadequate and that the world was inherently unsafe. His growing fear that he could never know who would harm him then sharpened his hypervigilance, making every delay a potential warning sign and every moment of quiet a threat he could not dismiss. Because he found it impossible to believe when others told him he was safe, his dread of harm only deepened, locking his mind into a cycle where his negative interpretations constantly amplified his threat monitoring. His editor eventually reassigned him to archival research, a concrete consequence of his withdrawal that further isolated him from the colleagues he needed. Now twenty-seven and recently engaged to his longtime partner, Elena, Dinh still works in journalism, but the beats he once loved have shrunk to the safety of his apartment. He takes the bus only when his editor demands it, standing near the doors with his eyes fixed on the dashboard, certain that the driver’s sudden brake or a fellow passenger’s shift in posture could unravel him. He avoids eating at newsroom staff lunches, telling himself he isn’t hungry while his stomach tightens from the silence he refuses to voice. When he lies awake checking the locks or staring at the ceiling, wondering if safety is real or just a temporary pause, he wonders if the trauma has permanently altered his capacity to trust anyone, including himself. What finally brought him into the clinic was a panic attack during a radio interview when the guest’s deep voice mirrored Mark’s cadence, leaving Dinh unable to speak or breathe for three full minutes. He hopes to break the knot of dread that grips his chest when he sees a man’s silhouette, and he fears that without intervention, the fear of harm and the weight of his own inadequacy will keep him permanently isolated.
